objectives: Describe the illusion of intelligence as the reading of a proxy as the ability itself.
Name the three words of the subject: proxy, evidence and ability.
Explain what a score measures well, and what it leaves out.
Compare six kinds of evidence of thinking ability, from weak to strong.
Use six steps to judge ability from real work instead of from a label.
Check your own judgement of yourself and of other people before you rate anybody's ability.

sections.body:
A **proxy** is a stand-in for the thing you want to know but cannot see directly. A test score stands in for ability. A certificate stands in for knowledge of a syllabus. A fast, confident answer stands in for understanding. The proxy is useful: it is cheap, standard and easy to compare. The illusion begins the moment the proxy is read as the thing itself.

Three words carry the whole idea. A **proxy** is the measurable stand-in. **Evidence** is the information that supports or weakens a claim about ability. **Ability** is the capacity to do a task well, in a real situation, under real conditions. A score is evidence. It is evidence of something narrow, and the narrowness is easy to lose.

The step that makes the illusion is short and fast. A number arrives, it is easy to read, and the reader supplies the rest. The number was high, so the person is capable. That feels like observation, but it is an inference. The evidence has been stretched from a mark to a mind.

The system pushes in the same direction. Certificates and scores are made to be legible and comparable, so they travel well between employers, schools and agencies. The person behind the mark becomes a mark with a name attached, and the mark travels much further than the person does.
examples: The certificate is evidence of an assessment, not evidence of ability.
A score is evidence of one performance on one day, so I treat it as one input.
That answer was fast and confident. Speed is not the same as understanding.
sections.heading: The illusion: reading a proxy as the thing itself

terms.example: The score is only a proxy; the ability itself is what the employer needs.
terms.gloss: A measurable stand-in for something you cannot see directly, such as a score standing in for ability.

terms.example: The written test is evidence of one performance, not of ability in general.
terms.gloss: Information that supports or weakens a claim.

terms.example: The ability to find the fault was there; the procedure had never been written down.
terms.gloss: The capacity to do a task well, in a real situation, under real conditions.

sections.body:
A score is a measurement, and it is a good measurement inside its own conditions. It is taken on one scale, under one set of instructions, on one day, with one set of questions. Inside those conditions it is precise enough to compare one candidate with another, one year with another, one site with another.

Two words describe the quality of a measurement, and they answer different questions. **Validity** asks: does this test measure what it claims to measure? A driving test full of theory questions can be valid for theory and weak for driving. **Reliability** asks: if the same person takes the same test again, do they get a similar result? A test can be reliable and still not valid for the job, which means the same mark every time about something else.

This part is worth saying plainly, because it is often skipped. A score is not noise, and it is not meaningless luck. It is a real measurement of a real thing under stated conditions, and it is cheap next to watching somebody work. It is also standard, which is the only reason it can be compared at all. Anyone who trusts evidence should keep the score and read it carefully.
examples: The test is reliable, but it is not valid for this job.
I am not dismissing the score; I am reading it for what it measured.
Same scale, same instructions, same day: that is what makes the number comparable.
sections.heading: What a score measures well

terms.example: The test was reliable but not valid for the work we do.
terms.gloss: The quality of a test that asks whether it measures what it claims to measure.

terms.example: Two markers gave the same result, so the marking was reliable.
terms.gloss: The quality of a measurement that gives a similar result when it is repeated.

sections.body:
The score is silent about the things that decide the work. It says nothing about whether the skill travels to a new situation. It says nothing about motivation, or about persistence on the day when the problem is hard. It says nothing about working with other people, and nothing about judgement when the information is incomplete and nobody can be asked.

**Transfer of learning** is the first of these: the ability to use what you learned in one situation in a different situation. A candidate can answer every question about a procedure and still stop at the first time the procedure differs in any way: another machine, another fault, another order of steps. A score taken in one situation says very little about that.

**Practice effect** is the second. When a test is taken more than once, the result often rises because the material has been seen before, not because the ability has grown. This is a well established finding in testing, and it changes how a second result should be read. Nerves work in the same way on the day itself: a bad day is not a bad person, and a good day is not a good person. A score always carries the day with it.

None of this makes a score worthless. It makes a score one measurement of one thing on one day, while a person is much larger than that. The distance between the two is where the illusion lives.
examples: The skill did not transfer: the procedure was the same, the situation was not.
The second result is higher, and the practice effect explains much of it.
A bad day at the test is not a verdict on the person.
sections.heading: What a score does not measure

terms.example: The training transferred well: the same method worked on a new line.
terms.gloss: The ability to use what you learned in one situation in a different situation.

terms.example: The second attempt scored higher, and the practice effect explains much of it.
terms.gloss: The rise in a test result that comes from having seen the material before.

sections.body:
Evidence of thinking ability comes in strengths. The order below is about closeness to the real work, not about how impressive the evidence looks. A certificate looks more serious than a piece of work, but it is further from the job.

Three words help you read the rows. A **norm** is the usual result of a group, so a number means little until you know what that group usually gets. **Discriminability** is the power of a test to separate the people who know the material from the people who do not. A **criterion** is the standard a result is compared against, and in hiring the criterion is the work the job requires, not the mark on the paper.
examples: What does the score mean against the norm for this test?
The certificate is evidence of the assessment; the work is evidence of the ability.
Let me compare the result with the criterion: what the job actually needs.
sections.heading: Evidence of thinking ability, from weak to strong

rows: The result of one assessment, taken under the conditions of that assessment.
Use it as one input, and ask what the assessment actually measured.
That a named assessment was completed on one syllabus, on one day.
Check the syllabus and the assessment, not the name on the certificate.
A confident answer in an interview
That the person can speak about the topic under the pressure of the moment.
Ask for the worked example behind the confident answer.
That the answer came quickly, which says little about whether it is right.
Never read speed as ability; check the answer itself.
The closest thing to the job that any evidence can offer.
Look for the decisions, the trade-offs and the reasons behind them.
The record of a mistake and its fix
How the person notices a problem, works out a cause, and changes the work.
Ask what went wrong and what changed afterwards.

terms.example: Compare the mark with the norm for that group, not with the mark alone.
terms.gloss: The usual result of a group, used as the point of comparison.

terms.example: A test that everybody passes has poor discriminability.
terms.gloss: The power of a test to separate the people who know the material from those who do not.

terms.example: The criterion is the work the job requires, not the mark on the certificate.
terms.gloss: The standard that a result is compared against.

sections.body:
The six steps below work on any judgement of ability: a hiring decision, a review, a handover, a promotion. The order matters. The task comes first, because without it every later step measures the wrong thing.

One rule runs through all six. You are not looking for a person who sounds right; you are looking for a person who does the work. The steps are slow on purpose, and the slow part is where the evidence is.
examples: Show me a real case, and talk me through what you did.
What went wrong there, and what did you change afterwards?
The label is not the check; the work is the check.
sections.heading: How to judge ability from evidence
steps: Look at the task, not at the person. Describe the job in real terms first: what must be produced, under what constraints, with what information, and how the result will be used.
Ask for a worked example, not a summary. A summary can be copied or memorised; a worked example shows the choices the person made and the reasons for them.
Watch the reasoning while it happens. Let the person think aloud through a real case, and note where they check their work, where they hesitate, and where they ask a question.
Ask about a mistake and what changed after it. The fix is stronger evidence than the first success, because it shows judgement applied after the facts arrived.
Change one condition and see if it transfers. Move the example into a new context, with a new constraint, and see whether the method survives the move.
Check the result against the task, not against the label. Compare the evidence with what the work requires, and write down the gap between them.

sections.body:
This warning is about the hardest case: your own judgement, and your judgement of other people. **Self-assessment** is the habit of rating your own work, and it is the least reliable evidence you have, because you know what you meant and where you struggled, and that knowledge changes how you read your own result. **Overestimation** is the same gap seen from the other side: you rate your ability above what it is, and the gap is invisible from inside.

There is a real finding behind this. David Dunning and John Kruger reported that people who know little about a subject tend to rate their own ability high, while experts on the same subject rate it low. How large that effect is, and how far it explains everyday mistakes, is still argued over. Do not build your policy on the size of it. The safe rule does not depend on the size: never rate ability from one performance, and never rate a person from a fast answer.

The opposite error exists too, and in a team it is the more expensive one. People who are strong often doubt themselves, especially when the work is new or when they are the newest person in the room. They hedge, they ask permission, they say they are not sure about work they have already done well. That is not humility; it is the same misreading of evidence, running the other way. The rule protects the strong and the weak alike.
examples: One result is not a rating of a person.
I would rather see the work than judge the answer.
Do not trust a fast answer, from anybody, including me.
sections.heading: Judging yourself, and judging other people

terms.example: Self-assessment told him he was ready; the job in front of him said otherwise.
terms.gloss: Judging your own work or your own ability.

terms.example: Her overestimation cost her the job she had already won in her head.
terms.gloss: Rating your ability above what it is.

sections.body:
These are the sentences that turn a score into a question about the work. Use them in a review, in a hiring discussion, or in a handover where somebody has to make a decision from a file of marks.

The middle ones are the useful ones. A score is a fact about an assessment, so it is easy to accept and hard to question. Ask a question about the work instead, and the score becomes one piece of information among several.
examples: The certificate shows the assessment was taken; it does not show the work.
Can we look at a real piece of your work and talk through the decisions?
The score tells me about the test. It does not tell me about this job.
What did you check before you made that call?
Tell me about a time it went wrong, and what you changed afterwards.
I would like to see the same skill in a different situation.
What result would count as good enough here?
I am not comparing you with the certificate. I am comparing the evidence with the job.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use in a review, a hiring discussion or a handover

sections.body:
A certificate is often described as proof of knowledge. What it actually proves is narrower: that a named person sat a named assessment, on one syllabus, on one day, and met the standard that assessment set. That is a real fact and it is worth something. It is a fact about an event, not about a person.

An employer still has to check three things. Whether the assessment resembles the work. Whether the person can do the work under the conditions of the work: time, pressure, colleagues, and information that does not arrive complete. And whether the evidence came from that person's own hands. None of these three is answered by the certificate itself.

This is why a portfolio of real work says more than a list of marks. Marks are compressed: one number stands for a year of work, and the number cannot show which decisions were hard. A portfolio keeps the decisions, the trade-offs, the mistakes and the fixes, and it lets a reader compare the evidence with the job instead of with a ranking. A list of marks is sorted by somebody else's criteria, and those criteria are not necessarily the criteria of the job in front of you.
examples: The certificate tells me the assessment was done; the portfolio tells me what you can do.
I would like to see the work under the conditions we actually have.
The marks were sorted by the exam board, not by what this job needs.
sections.heading: Grades, certificates and hiring

item.summary: A grade, a certificate and a fast answer are proxies: cheap, standard stand-ins for ability. After reading this you can name what a score really measures, separate evidence from the conclusion drawn from it, compare six kinds of evidence from weak to strong, and use six steps to judge ability from real work instead of from a label.
item.title: The Illusion of Intelligence: When a Grade Is Mistaken for Ability
